<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Accurate multiplex analysis of microRNAs (miRNAs) remains constrained by enzymatic amplification, spectral crosstalk, and instrumental complexity. Herein, we report a conceptually distinct PhC-SQ platform that integrates photonic crystal (PhC) structural encoding with S9.6-mediated universal recognition for amplification-free multiplex miRNA detection. PhC microspheres act as structural color barcodes for target encoding, while quantum dots (QDs) enriched at the microsphere interface serve as fluorescent reporters. Target miRNAs hybridize with surface-bound DNA probes to form DNA/RNA duplexes, which are recognized by the S9.6 antibody. Subsequent biotin–streptavidin assembly recruits QDs, enabling interfacial fluorescence enrichment and enhanced sensitivity without enzymatic amplification. By decoupling encoding from readout, the platform eliminates spectral crosstalk and enables accurate multiplexing. A dual-mode readout, combining confocal quantification with direct UV visualization, further supports point-of-care applicability. Validation in cellular samples shows good agreement with RT-PCR. Overall, this work establishes a structural encoding-universal recognition-interfacial signal enrichment strategy for robust and field-deployable multiplex miRNA detection.</jats:p>
title:
Structural Encoding-decoupled Universal Recognition
Enables Amplification-free Multiplex miRNA Detection

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Voltammetric solid-contact ion-selective electrodes (SC-ISEs) exhibit electrochemical responses that arise from the coupling of heterogeneous electron transfer at the electrode−membrane interface with ion transfer at the membrane−sample boundary. In this work, a novel theoretical framework is developed for voltammetric SC-ISEs based on thin membranes, capturing the intrinsic consequences of coupling two polarized interfaces in series under markedly different mass-transport conditions in the membrane and solution phases. The theory describes the current/charge−potential−time responses and the corresponding interfacial potentials and dynamic ion and redox-species concentrations, accounting for the effects of membrane and solution composition, membrane thickness, and experimental timescale. Besides, the theory enables quantitative analysis of experimental voltammetric outcomes. A systematic classification of cyclic voltammetry (CV) responses is obtained in terms of three dimensionless parameters that quantify ion availability in the sample solution relative to the confined membrane. Simple relationships for peak positions and practical diagnostic criteria based on CV shape and scan-rate dependence are derived to verify thin-membrane conditions and the absence of kinetic or ohmic limitations, identifying indeed whether charge compensation proceeds via ion release or uptake.</jats:p>
title: When Two Interfaces Meet: A Unified Theory for Thin-Membrane Voltammetric Ion Selective Electrodes

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Peak overlap limits chemical assignment in drift-tube ion mobility spectrometry (DT-IMS). Diffusion broadening is commonly modeled with symmetric Gaussian kernels, although a fixed detector records ion first-passage times. We developed an inverse-Gaussian-Nernst-Townsend-Einstein (IG-NTE) deconvolution framework in which the point-spread function (PSF) follows an inverse-Gaussian distribution and its temporal width is constrained by instrument settings through the NTE relation. The resulting drift-time-dependent measurement operator was inverted by nonnegative Richardson-Lucy iteration without peak-width calibration or specification of component number. In simulations, relative to a Gaussian kernel, IG-NTE deconvolution reduced the average full-residual root-mean-square value by 11.4%, the right-tail residual by 18.1%, and the mean absolute peak-area deviation from 5.10% to 1.19%. Applied to a 63Ni DT-IMS instrument, the method separated ethyl 2-methylpentanoate and 1,8-cineole responses 0.040 ms apart while retaining 2,6-di-tert-butylpyridine (DTBP) as a single-component control. It also recovered paired alkyl-pyrazine mobility features consistent with protonation site- and hydration-dependent collision cross sections. In the negative mode, dichloromethane-derived chloride responses assigned to 35Cl− and 37Cl− exhibited a 3.08:1 area ratio and were supported by GC-TOF-MS. These results show that detector-domain transport modeling can improve the effective reconstructed resolution of diffusion-broadened DT-IMS spectra without hardware modification, provided that controls and forward residual analysis are used to assess reconstruction artifacts.</jats:p>
title: Physically Constrained Inverse-Gaussian Deconvolution of Diffusion-Broadened Drift-Tube Ion Mobility Spectra

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Inherited dyslipidemias, including familial hypercholesterolemia (FH) and sitosterolemia (STSL), present overlapping clinical manifestations but require distinct therapeutic interventions. Current diagnosis relies on genetic sequencing and mass spectrometry-based sterol profiling, which are accurate but costly, time-consuming, and unsuitable for large-scale first-line screening. Infrared (IR) microspectroscopy offers a rapid, label-free alternative for biochemical phenotyping; however, its clinical application is challenged by the spatial heterogeneity of biological samples and spectral variability. Here, we present an IR microspectroscopic phenotyping framework for rapid screening and etiological stratification of inherited dyslipidemias. The framework combines multi-pixel IR microspectroscopy, batch-effect correction, and participant-level spectral integration to achieve reproducible cross-batch phenotyping while preserving disease-associated biochemical signatures. Quantitative models predicted FH-associated lipid biomarkers, whereas qualitative classifiers identified STSL-associated sterol biomarkers. A cascade decision framework integrating IR-based phenotypic classification with biomarker profiling further enabled etiological discrimination among healthy controls, FH, and STSL. The framework achieved an average participant-level sensitivity of approximately 93% and yielded detection rates of 97.7% for FH and 85.7% for STSL, compared with 93.2% and 60.7%, respectively, with conventional clinical screening. Co-importance and consensus feature analyses identified 2837 cm−1 as a prominent discriminatory spectral feature. Measurements of β-sitosterol reference standards revealed a characteristic absorption band near 2834 cm−1, supporting a possible association between this spectral region and β-sitosterol-related biochemical variation. This internally validated proof-of-concept study supports the potential of IR microspectroscopy for rapid etiological stratification of inherited dyslipidemias, complementing genetic sequencing and mass spectrometry.</jats:p>
title: Rapid Screening and Etiological Stratification of Inherited Dyslipidemias by Infrared Microspectroscopy

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Two-dimensional Ruddlesden−Popper (2D RP) perovskites hold immense promise as light-harvesting photoactive materials for photoelectrochemical (PEC) bioanalysis, yet their poor aqueous durability and suboptimal charge-carrier dynamics severely restrict PEC sensing implementation. Herein, we report a dual-functional strategy that simultaneously addresses both challenges through the in-situ construction of a Z-scheme heterojunction, (BA)2PbI4−Pb(OH)2 (BA = butylammonium), via Lewis base vapor diffusion. The Pb(OH)2 barrier formed during synthesis acts as a robust protective shield that preserves the perovskite’s structural integrity, while the intimate Z-scheme heterointerface constructed in the heterojunction remains functional and continues to accelerate spatial charge separation even after three years of immersion in ultrapure water, as corroborated by electron paramagnetic resonance spectroscopy, photo-assisted Kelvin probe force microscopy, and density functional theory calculations. To further amplify the PEC signal, we engineer a circular DNA scaffold-supported tripedal DNA walker powered by self-priming polymerization, eliminating the requirement for exogenous primers in traditional polymerase-driven DNA nanomachines. Target-triggered autonomous walking of the tripedal DNA nanomachine continuously disassembles surface-tethered hairpin tracks, drastically mitigating interfacial steric hindrance and yielding prominent photocurrent enhancement. Synergizing the ultra-stable Z-scheme RP perovskite photoelectrode with the primer-free DNA walker, the integrated PEC sensing platform achieves ultrasensitive quantification of acetamiprid with a wide linear range spanning 10−13 to 10−6 M. This work establishes a new paradigm for rationally designing aqueous-stable perovskites and coupling them with intelligent molecular devices, paving the way for high-performance PEC sensing platforms.</jats:p>
title: Synergistic Integration of Water-Stable 2D Perovskite Heterojunctions and Self-Priming DNA Walkers for Sensitive Photoelectrochemical Biosensing
